topic: Research: VS Code 1.115 Agent-Native Development: What Changed and What It Means

key_points: Official VS Code 1.115 release date: April 8, 2026.
Introduces Visual Studio Code Agents, a preview companion app that ships with VS Code Insiders.
Agents app supports parallel sessions across repos, with each session isolated in its own worktree.
Developers can monitor progress, review diffs inline, leave feedback, and create pull requests from the app.
Existing VS Code customizations carry over, including custom instructions, prompt files, custom agents, MCP servers, hooks, plugins, and themes.
Integrated browser improvements include clearer browser tool-call labels, links to target tabs, deferred results for long-running Playwright scripts, fewer duplicate tabs, and macOS pinch-to-zoom.
Terminal improvements include a new send_to_terminal tool for background terminals and experimental background terminal notifications.
Frames 1.115 as Microsoft moving VS Code from an editor with AI features toward an agent execution environment.
Highlights the operational value of isolated worktrees for running multiple agent sessions without conflicts.
Emphasizes review and governance: inline diffs, feedback loops, and PR creation are treated as core agent workflow infrastructure.
Calls browser transparency, long-running Playwright support, and background terminal interaction reliability improvements for real agentic workflows.
Includes analyst framing that visibility and control set the ceiling for safe autonomous development.
News-style summary focused on the VS Code Agents app as the headline feature of 1.115.
Notes that VS Code Agents is available as an Insiders preview rather than a stable default app.
Explains that developers can run agentic tasks across multiple projects in parallel.
Highlights review features: progress tracking, inline diffs, feedback, and pull request creation.
Mentions background terminal improvements as the second major agent-oriented part of the release.
Connects VS Code 1.115 and 1.116 into a broader weekly-release push around chat, agents, and Copilot workflows.
Explains that 1.115 added the preview Agents app and more direct terminal control for agents.
Notes that 1.116 continued the same direction with persistent agent debug logs and Copilot CLI reasoning controls.
Useful competitor angle: VS Code is building continuity across release cycles, not shipping a one-off AI feature.
Positioning angle: Microsoft is lowering friction by making Copilot-related capabilities more integrated in VS Code.
Official positioning page describes VS Code as an open platform for AI agents.
Highlights multiple agent modes: local interactive agents, cloud agents, Copilot CLI, and third-party agents.
States developers can run third-party agents from Anthropic, OpenAI, and others directly alongside VS Code tools.
Emphasizes model choice, including dozens of models and bring-your-own API keys.
Lists customization themes that matter for agent-native teams: MCP servers, skills, custom instructions, planning agents, memory, subagents, sandboxing, auto-approvals, and enterprise policies.

stats.fact: VS Code 1.115 was released on April 8, 2026, with the VS Code Agents preview app, integrated browser updates, and terminal-tool improvements as the release highlights.
The VS Code Agents preview app is currently available through VS Code Insiders and ships alongside it, rather than requiring a separate install.
In Stack Overflow's 2025 Developer Survey, 84% of respondents were using or planning to use AI tools in development, up from 76% the prior year.
Stack Overflow's 2025 survey reported that 51% of professional developers use AI tools daily.
Stack Overflow's 2025 survey found that 66% of developers were frustrated by AI solutions that are almost right but not quite, and 45.2% cited time-consuming debugging of AI-generated code.
GitHub's Octoverse 2025 reported more than 1.1 million public repositories using an LLM SDK, with 693,867 of those projects created in the prior 12 months, a 178% year-over-year increase.
GitHub's Octoverse 2025 reported that nearly 80% of new developers on GitHub use GitHub Copilot within their first week.
GitHub's Octoverse 2025 reported that developers merged 518.7 million pull requests, up 29% year over year.
GitHub's Octoverse 2025 reported that more than 180 million developers now build on GitHub, and more than 36 million developers joined in one year.
The current VS Code Agents feature page positions VS Code as supporting local, cloud, CLI, and third-party agent workflows, including agents from Anthropic, OpenAI, and others.

angles: Agent-native development is not just chat in the editor; VS Code 1.115 adds the execution scaffolding agents need: isolated worktrees, parallel sessions, monitoring, review, and PR handoff.
The biggest product signal is the separate Agents app: Microsoft is treating agent work as a session-management problem, not just a better autocomplete problem.

The release matters because it attacks the practical failure modes of agentic coding: losing track of diffs, conflicting parallel changes, opaque browser actions, brittle Playwright runs, and terminals that stall waiting for input.
The app is still preview-only in VS Code Insiders, so the right recommendation is to evaluate it for agent-heavy workflows while keeping stable VS Code for day-to-day production development.
Teams should read the release through a governance lens: agent productivity only scales when review, observability, isolation, and approval controls are part of the workflow.
VS Code is converging with AI-first IDEs and coding agents by becoming an open agent host that can run Copilot, CLI agents, cloud agents, and third-party agents in the same developer environment.
The Stack Overflow trust gap gives the article tension: adoption is already mainstream, but developers still need better review and debugging affordances, which is exactly where 1.115 invests.

A useful takeaway for engineering managers: the feature set favors multi-repo maintenance, test generation, refactors, migrations, and async task delegation more than pair-programming-style code completion.
